item.title: How Exercise May Change the Brain’s Emotional Networks
item.description:
Depression

How Exercise May Change the Brain’s Emotional Networks

Exercise may eventually take on a role in mental health care.

Posted August 25, 2026

Key points
  • A single session of low- or high-intensity exercise changes mood and communication between brain regions.
  • Both forms of exercise produced a substantial increase in positive mood.
  • High-intensity exercise also appeared to strengthen brain areas altered in people with depression.

Exercise changes far more than the muscles and heart. A single bout can sharpen attention, alter stress hormones, and, for many people, improve how they feel. Scientists have known about this emotional lift for years. What remains less clear is what happens inside the brain as mood begins to change.

A recent study from the University Hospital Bonn offers a glimpse into that process. Twenty highly trained young men completed three separate sessions: low-intensity interval exercise, high-intensity interval exercise, and a control session in which they sat quietly on a bicycle. Before and after each session, the participants rated their mood and underwent brain imaging while resting. The results indicated that exercise may help preserve, and perhaps strengthen, communication between brain regions that help balance emotional reactions with inward reflection.

A Noticeable Lift in Mood

Positive mood rose significantly after both exercise sessions. The improvement was large after low-intensity exercise and similarly large after high-intensity exercise. High-intensity exercise produced a somewhat greater increase, although the difference between the two exercise levels did not reach the study’s threshold for statistical certainty. Sitting quietly produced no comparable rise in positive mood.

The picture became more complicated when the participants rated negative feelings. Negative mood actually fell after the resting condition, while neither exercise condition produced a statistically clear decrease. Anxiety also remained largely unchanged across all three conditions.

That may sound surprising, but the participants entered the study with very low levels of depression, anxiety, and negative mood. They were also highly fit. There was therefore relatively little distress for exercise to reduce in the first place. The more interesting question was whether the improvement in positive mood had a visible counterpart inside the brain.

A Conversation Between Two Parts of the Brain

The study focused on the amygdala, a small structure deep within the brain that plays an important role in evaluating emotionally important information. Fear attracts much of the attention in discussions of the amygdala, but its role extends well beyond fear. It helps the brain decide what matters emotionally.

The team then examined how activity in the amygdala rose and fell alongside activity elsewhere in the brain. At first, the results looked modest. An analysis across the entire brain found no significant exercise-related changes in communication with the amygdala. The study also failed to reproduce some earlier findings involving the insula and temporal regions.

One region, however, stood out. The precuneus lies toward the back of the brain and forms an important part of a network that becomes active when the mind turns inward. It participates in self-reflection, memory, and the construction of our internal experience. Growing evidence also links it to the way we regulate emotions and direct attention.

Under normal circumstances, activity in the amygdala and precuneus often moves in opposite directions. When activity in one rises, activity in the other tends to fall. Scientists call this an anticorrelation.

During the control condition, this opposing relationship became weaker after participants spent time sitting on the bicycle. Exercise prevented that decline. High-intensity exercise went further, showing a tendency toward an even stronger opposing relationship between the amygdala and precuneus. Three areas within the precuneus showed significant differences when the high-intensity session was compared with the control condition.

Why the Precuneus Matters

The importance of this finding becomes clearer when viewed through the lens of depression. People with major depression often show abnormal activity in the brain network that includes the precuneus. This network helps generate self-focused thought, and excessive activity within it has been linked to rumination, the repetitive cycle of dwelling on distressing thoughts.

Some studies have also found that the normal opposing relationship between the amygdala and precuneus becomes weaker in depression. In certain patients, the two regions may even begin moving together instead of in opposition.

High-intensity exercise appeared to reinforce a pattern of brain communication commonly seen in healthy individuals and sometimes disrupted in affective illness. Earlier work from the same group also found that months of repeated aerobic exercise strengthened this same opposing relationship between the amygdala and precuneus.

Exercise for the Brain

Physical activity is often described as medicine for the heart, muscles, and metabolism. Its effects on the brain may prove just as important. A workout may be capable of briefly changing the biological state in which thought and emotion occur.

The next step is not to declare one exercise intensity superior to another. It is to understand which forms of activity produce useful brain changes, how long those changes last, and whether repeated exercise can reshape emotional networks in people who need that help most. If that proves true, exercise may eventually take on an even more precise role in mental health care. It could become one more way to influence the biology of emotional regulation through an intervention that is inexpensive, widely available, and already known to benefit the body.

The most promising lesson from this study is, therefore, not that a hard workout makes us happier. It is that even a single period of physical activity may leave a measurable trace in the networks through which the brain organizes emotion. Understanding that trace may help explain why movement has such a powerful influence on how we feel.

item.title: Climate Change Is Changing the Conditions in Which We Parent
item.description:
Environment

Climate Change Is Changing the Conditions in Which We Parent

What extreme heat tells us about stress, child abuse, and prevention.

Posted August 25, 2026

Key points
  • Extreme heat can add stress to families already stretched thin.
  • Children rely on regulated adults, but heat and stress can make regulation harder.
  • More research is needed on climate change as a potential child-maltreatment risk.
Source: Cavan Images - Offset / Shutterstock

This post is Part 2 of a series. Part 1 can be found here.

Grand Union, 1989

My son was two that summer. I had an old Volvo with a broken clutch we couldn't afford to properly fix. We had rigged it with a vise grip. Like the mother at Target, I didn't have AC either. And as I left the store, I was pretty sure I had just bounced a check buying groceries.

It was July. My son refused to get into his car seat. When I tried to put him in, he started hitting me in the face. An older woman came over. "Just swat him back," she said. "Or he'll grow up to be a brat." I was horrified. I would never hit a 2-year-old. But I've thought about that woman since the afternoon at Target. What did I look like to her? I was trying to control my voice, using that low, slow way mothers sometimes talk when they are trying very hard not to lose their patience. I was sweating through my shirt. My face was red from embarrassment and from being slapped. And my son was not giving in.

Eventually, I got him buckled in. He screamed all 25 minutes home. Our apartment didn't have AC either. When we got inside, I put him in his playpen and went into the bathroom and cried. I knew enough then to understand that when my frustration became too much, I needed to make sure he was safe and walk away for a few minutes. Later, we found out my son had strep throat.

Thirty-seven years later, I watched another mother trying to get a sick child into a car on another brutally hot day. That was when this stopped feeling like an abstract research question.

What Happens When the Parent Needs Regulating, Too?

Psychologists use the term co-regulation to describe something parents do all the time. Young children are still learning how to handle big emotions. An adult helps them settle. Except sometimes the adult isn't settled either. I remember that feeling. Your child is screaming, and you know you are supposed to stay calm, except the checking account is overdrawn and the car might break down and sweat is running down your back, and now your 2-year-old is hitting you in the face. Knowing what to do helped me that day. Put him somewhere safe. Walk away. Cry in the bathroom if you need to. Come back.

Heat doesn't make someone an abusive parent. Most parents get through miserably hot days without hurting their children. But heat can make an already hard day harder. Maybe neither you nor your child slept well because the apartment never cooled down. The playground equipment is too hot to touch. The pool isn't an option because your child has an ear infection. Four children have been inside together all day and are fighting and tired of each other. And maybe there is no one to call. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention identifies a number of things that can help protect children from abuse and neglect: parents who are able to cope with everyday stress, strong social support, access to economic help, and communities with resources families can actually use.

What Else Aren't We Seeing?

We have become accustomed to thinking about what extreme heat can do to a child's body. We worry about dehydration and heat illness. We close playgrounds and cancel practices when temperatures become dangerous. We know that wildfire smoke can affect children's lungs and that floods and hurricanes can displace families. But what about what happens inside families?

The research is still developing, and there is a great deal we don't know. We need to understand much more about how extreme heat, disrupted sleep, financial strain, displacement, loss of routines, isolation, and reduced access to services affect parents and children together.

We need more research in the United States. We need to know which families are most vulnerable and why. We need to know which supports actually reduce risk. And we need to understand whether some of the interventions we already use to protect people from the effects of climate change might also help prevent child maltreatment.

Cooling centers may be part of that. So might utility assistance, accessible childcare, mental health services, social connection, parent education, and respite for exhausted caregivers. But I don't think we know enough yet to make a neat list and call it prevention. What we do know is that climate change reaches much farther into children's lives than the temperature outside.

I didn't see an abusive mother at Target. I saw a mother whose ability to cope was being tested by one thing after another: four young children, a sick child, oppressive heat, no air-conditioning at home, and one less option when the pool became unavailable. I recognized something in her because 37 years earlier, under different circumstances, I had felt my own patience being tested on a hot day with a sick 2-year-old. Neither story proves anything about climate change and child abuse. The research is what made me realize the question was worth asking.

If climate change can increase some of the conditions associated with child maltreatment while also weakening some of the things that protect children and families, then we need to understand that relationship much better. Not so we can blame overwhelmed parents for what happens on the hottest days, but so we can recognize another place where prevention may be possible. Climate change is already changing childhood. We need to understand what that means not only for children's bodies and the planet they will inherit, but for the families raising them now. And if there are ways to reduce the added risk before a parent or a child reaches a breaking point, we should be looking for them.

item.title: 'Inat': The Positive Side of Negative Motivation
item.description:
Motivation

'Inat': The Positive Side of Negative Motivation

How doubt, defiance, and the desire to prove others wrong can fuel achievement.

Posted August 25, 2026

Key points
  • A feeling of being underestimated can become a source of identity, resilience, and disciplined effort.
  • Doubt and anger can spark remarkable persistence, but relying on them too heavily may undermine contentment.
  • Sustainable achievement requires transforming the urge to prove others wrong into goals guided by values.

We often talk about motivation for achievement as if it is fundamentally positive. We imagine the successful person driven by curiosity, passion, confidence, and a clear vision of the future. Another popular belief is that competition should motivate by itself: put people on the same court, or in the same workplace, and the desire to win will supposedly provide enough energy.

Both assumptions are incomplete.

The recent documentary Novak Djokovic: The Wolf in Winter offers a more complex picture. Djokovic, perhaps the greatest male tennis player of all time, discusses the concept of inat (a Serbian word of Arabic origin): a blend of defiance, stubbornness, pride, and determination to prove others—or oneself—wrong. He reveals in the documentary that his career was shaped not only by ambition, but also by doubt, anger, and a refusal to accept other people’s judgments about his abilities, choices and limitations. As his former coach, Andre Agassi, remarks in the documentary, Djokovic needs anger and fear to operate at his peak—love and happiness alone take away his edge.

The Gladiator
Source: AI Generated

This raises important questions: How useful can negative motivation be? Can it provide an extra “edge” in highly competitive settings and is it sustainable?

Motivation Is Not Always Positive

Motivation for achievement has two broad directions. We may move toward a desirable outcome, such as success, mastery, or recognition. Or we may move away from an undesirable one, such as failure, shame, rejection, or status loss.

Psychologists Andrew Elliot and Marcy Church distinguish between approach and avoidance forms of motivation. People can pursue achievement either by trying to demonstrate competence or by trying not to appear incompetent. These motives may produce similar behavior—studying, training, working late—but they can feel very different internally (Elliot & Church, 1997).

article continues after advertisement

The psychologist Gavin Kilduff (2014) shows that in competitive situations with a long relational history, individuals may experience an acute spike in motivation, as the driving force shifts from a positive goal ("I want to win the prize") to an avoidance/loss-prevention frame ("I cannot lose to them"). The "whatever it takes" mindset, however, is associated with increase in unsportsmanlike conduct.

“Negative” forms of motivation can be very powerful. Doubt can push us to prepare more thoroughly. Dissatisfaction can propel exceptional persistence, even if it is often experienced as a psychological burden. But the same doubt that keeps someone practicing in pursuit of success and recognition can also make it difficult to feel content with one’s achievements.

The Psychology of Defiance

The concept of inat embodies the refusal to be defined by another person’s expectations. For Djokovic, it was the need to establish himself against powerful and highly popular rivals and, at times, against an audience that seemed more comfortable with the victories of these rivals.

This can generate identity-based motivation. The task becomes more than winning a match. Success becomes a way of answering a fundamental question: What am I really worth? It is through this question that one separates intrinsic worth (who one is) from extraneous value (what one produces, earns, or achieves).

article continues after advertisement

Many people recognize this experience in less dramatic terms. A student works harder after being rebuked by a teacher. An employee persists after being passed over for promotion. Achievement becomes a way to defend a sense of self. Such motivation can be powerful because it links effort to identity. The person is not merely pursuing an achievement; they are resisting an imposed definition of themselves.

Competition Is Not Enough

The belief that competition automatically motivates also needs qualification. Competition can provide a clear objective, immediate feedback, and an uplifting challenge. But it can also undermine engagement when it feels controlling, demeaning, or too focused on winning.

Research informed by self-determination theory shows that competitive settings can either support or diminish intrinsic motivation. Competition is more likely to energize people when it provides useful information about competence without threatening their autonomy. When it becomes pressure—“Win at all costs”—motivation can become brittle and anxiety-driven (Reeve & Deci, 1996).

This applies well to Djokovic’s competitiveness. He does not appear motivated only by the skill of the opponent. He is motivated by what the opponent represents: doubt, resistance, and an opportunity to test his identity. For another person, the same competitive context might produce withdrawal rather than effort. Competition is not a universal fuel. Its effects depend on how the individual interprets it, on its interaction with identity-level processes.

The Appeal and Danger of Negative Motivation

Negative motivation can be useful when it is converted into specific, disciplined action. Anger can become preparation. Fear can become planning. The desire to prove someone wrong can become persistence. It is especially likely to be helpful when there is a meaningful goal, when the challenge is specific in nature, and effort is directed toward improvement, not revenge.

The danger, however, is that a person may become too dependent on opposition as a source of motivation. If every accomplishment must defeat a critic and every victory is a rebuttal, a state of equanimity can feel like surrender. Djokovic’s own reflections capture this tension. He speaks of being driven by doubt while also feeling imprisoned by the demand to keep meeting lofty standards.

Negative motivation can incite remarkable achievement while making contentment appear ever more distant. It may encourage the belief that respite or emotional balance is evidence of weakness.

A More Balanced View

The psychology of achievement is not a choice between positive and negative motivation. Most people are moved by a mixture of both. We pursue success and avoid failure. We feel curiosity, ambition, fear, anger, and hope—sometimes all at once.

article continues after advertisement

Opposition can become energy, but that energy requires direction. Defiance may start the engine, but values and sober judgment must steer the vehicle.

We may occasionally need fear to prepare, or doubt to persist. But a balanced life eventually needs additional drivers: interest, autonomy, and social relationships. As Ryan and Deci (2017) argue, sustainable motivation is more likely when action also satisfies psychological needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness. As the documentary illustrates, a loving family and a healthy lifestyle can provide the needed counterweight to the intense drive for achievement.

The most constructive form of defiance may just be to become independent of others' judgment.
